source: Royal Government of Cambodia, General Directorate of Agriculture (GDA) / Boosting Food Production Program (PMO), "ខែ្សសង្វាក់ផលិតកម្ម ដំណាំពោតនៅកម្ពុជា" (Corn Production Value Chain in Cambodia), 2017
text:
Corn (maize) is an annual grass plant. A mature corn plant typically has a stalk 3 meters tall, though some varieties bred for animal-feed leaf harvest can reach 12 meters. Wild-type stalks are about 20 nodes tall with an average internode length of about 18 cm. Corn leaves are broad, up to 5 cm wide and about 120 cm long, alternating on opposite sides of the stalk.

The corn plant is monoecious, bearing separate male and female flower structures on the same plant. The male tassel forms at the top of the stalk, while the female ear (silk-bearing) structures form from buds at the leaf-stem junctions along the stalk, roughly 2-3 leaf nodes below the top of the plant. A healthy stalk can support 1-2 ears; each ear has 8 rows of kernels at minimum, and rows are typically an even number. An ear can be up to 18-20 cm long with as many as 60 rows of kernels. The silk (the fine threads at the ear tip that catch pollen) can grow to enormous relative length, sometimes described as growing several inches per day during flowering, and only reaches its full length once pollinated.

Key plant parts (per the document's labeled botanical diagram): tassel floret, glume, anthers, tassel, flag leaf, tassel internode, silks, ears, ear wing, leaf blade, leaf sheath, tiller, brace roots, and roots.

Corn originated roughly 10,000 years ago from wild teosinte grass, first domesticated by native peoples in the Balsas River valley region of Mexico. It later spread throughout the Americas, including into the Kansas/Nebraska plains region and the Sonoran desert areas of Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado in the United States, as well as the Andes region of South America (cited to Gibson & Benson, 2002 and Karl, 2013/2015 in the source document).
